subtopic: TWELFTH ANNIVERSARY OF SIGNING OF CHARTER

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: TWELFTH ANNIVERSARY OF SIGNING OF CHARTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with the leave of the house may I mention the fact that today is the twelfth anniversary of the signing of the charter of the United Nations. Canadians generally are joining with the other nations of the world in observing the anniversary of an organization which plays such a great role in the world of today. At the entrance to the parliament buildings are displayed the 82 flags of the member nations of the United Nations. The United Nations flag is being flown from the eastern flag pole of the centre block. This day represents an anniversary of an institution that we, as Canadians, believe to be necessary for the preservation and maintenance of peace. To that end Canada, in company with the other member nations, joins in a rededication to its principles.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: TWELFTH ANNIVERSARY OF SIGNING OF CHARTER
speechtext:
I am sure all hon. members read with interest the statement that was issued by the Prime Minister earlier today in connection with the twelfth anniversary of the coming into force of the charter of the United Nations. We have all listened with some emotion to the references the Prime Minister has made to that anniversary. I think it is fortunate that in this country the Canadian people generally have regarded the attitude of the Canadian government
toward that organization as something that was not the subject of any political partisanship, but that it has the unanimous support of the Canadian people because of the aims and ideals of that great organization.
It is now 12 years since the charter became operative. Not all the hopes of the right hon. gentleman and others who were with me at the time the charter was under discussion at San Francisco have been realized. Nevertheless I think there will be general agreement that it has served a useful purpose, and that it is still one of the main hopes of most of civilized humanity for the maintenance of as peaceful conditions in this troubled world as are possible under the present circumstances.

subtopic: TWELFTH ANNIVERSARY OF SIGNING OF CHARTER
speechtext:
I am
quite sure that there is unanimity, both in the House of Commons and in the country, regarding the recognition of this day and the signing of the charter of the United Nations. Those of us who had the privilege of being present at the San Francisco conference will remember the great hopes we had for the future under the United Nations charter. Those hopes have not all been realized. Nonetheless, it is better to have had a place where men of diverse views, representing nations with many interests, could get together and talk their problems out than to indulge in a shooting war.
In looking to the future, we can all hope the United Nations will fulfil its functions much better in the future than it has in the past. I have no doubt it has already played a great part in preserving the peace of the world and in bringing help to the underdeveloped countries and the less privileged nations of the world. I have no doubt it will continue to do that, and will serve mankind better in the future than it has in the past.

subtopic: TWELFTH ANNIVERSARY OF SIGNING OF CHARTER
speechtext:
I am sure there is unanimity of hopes and wishes, perhaps even of dreams throughout Canada and particularly throughout this house concerning the United Nations. I am very glad to add my voice to those who have already spoken in this chamber today in connection with this twelfth anniversary of the putting in force of the United Nations charter. It is true that the international organization that was born 12 years ago has not fulfilled all the hopes and dreams we had concerning it. There were weaknesses in the charter to begin with, and those weaknesses have

Proposed Legislation
been intensified over the years, in the opinion of many people. Nevertheless it appears to be the only international forum that we have in existence where the nations of the world can meet and talk out their problems rather than resorting to a shooting war.
Recognizing that fact, we all must express the hope that the work of the United Nations will become much more effective in the years ahead.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minisier of Trade and Commerce) moved

speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the making of advances on account of initial payments for grain produced in the designated area, as defined in the Canadian Wheat Board Act, prior to delivery thereof upon undertakings by the producers thereof to deliver the grain to the Canadian wheat board; and to provide for the costs, expenses and other financial obligations required in the making of such advances; such measure to include such further related and consequential provisions as are necessary to give effect to the foregoing.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Courtemanche in the chair.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution is the first of a series of resolutions introducing measures which will be for the benefit of the people of Canada. This is the first item of our legislative program, and it is designed to permit prairie farmers to receive advance payment for the grain they can expect to deliver this year. The legislation is necessary because of the large surplus of wheat which has been accumulated in recent years due to a number of factors such as larger than average crops, a reduction in exports

Grain
because of the loss of former markets, increased productivity per acre, subsidized competition from other wheat exporting countries, and so on.
The facts of the grain problem are that on August 1 of this year there was in Canada in storage in country and terminal elevators and in transit about 400 million bushels of wheat. An additional 300 million bushels was estimated by the dominion bureau of statistics to be held on farms, making a total carryover of 700 million bushels. That constitutes a substantial legacy from the past.
The new crop year was commenced on August 1, and the estimate of production for 1957-58 is about 350 million bushels. With the elevators crammed to capacity the prairie farmer is at the present time in the unhappy position of having good quality wheat available but little or no opportunity to deliver to the elevator and, therefore, no prospect of receiving in the fall the cash return he requires from his year's operation and the cash return that he might reasonably expect. Through no fault of his own, and due to a situation beyond his control, the prairie farmer cannot get immediately the cash he needs for his farming expenses and daily requirements.
It is to meet that requirement, that immediate need, that the legislation about to be put before the house has been prepared. An active and vigorous selling program is in progress. There is no relaxation of our efforts to dispose of our stocks of wheat at a fair return to the farmer. At the second reading stage of the bill I will discuss our sales program as well as other aspects of our wheat economy. However, hon. members may be interested in the situation at the moment, and I have promised the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) that I will give an answer to his question the other day on that subject. But hon. members may have noticed an accurate report in the Gazette this morning which was headlined "Canada Wheat Leads the World" and which reads as follows:
Canada led the world in wheat exports in August, though the amount shipped was slightly below that of last year. This was the first time in tour years that Canada has topped the United States in wheat exports in the opening month ol the new crop year. Canadian shipments totalled 27,200,000 bushels, down from 29,300,000 shipped in August last year, but above the 10-year average of 20,400,000 bushels.
That report comes from the dominion bureau of statistics.
The cash advance is not a hand-out or a subsidy to western farmers. All we are proposing is a cash advance on grain that will be delivered later, in the ensuing months.

We have no reason to doubt that the grain will be delivered, that space will become available in the elevators, and that exports will continue. The grain export trade of Canada is proceeding actively. There will be used up within Canada during the 12-month period from August 1, 1957, to July 31, 1958, at least 150 million bushels of wheat in one way or another, and there will be exported from Canada approximately 300 million bushels. That means that the equivalent of this year's crop will be all used up and, in addition, 100 million bushels of the carryover from preceding years.
But we cannot expect the prairie farmer to wait six months or a year before he gets some cash. While he is waiting to make delivery of his grain we consider that he should have some money to tide him over. The scheme we propose has been made as simple as possible. For many years the farmer has been delivering his grain on a quota system, receiving an initial payment from the elevator agent and producing his permit book to have the transaction recorded. The same system will be continued. The permit book will be produced, the elevator agent will make the advance and record the transaction, and the wheat board will keep accurate flies concerning each farmer's receipts in advance. The only differences are that the actual delivery of the grain will be made later, when elevator space becomes available, and the advance will, of course, be less than the initial payment.
Let us follow the procedure further. When elevator space becomes available the farmer will make his delivery, and one-half the value of the quantity of grain delivered will be applied to reducing the advance he has received. At each delivery the farmer will receive some cash so that he will not return home empty handed. Then, further, this fall he will get full return of the unit quota which is presently being delivered. Cash advances will apply on the 6-bushel quota which the wheat board considers will be applicable for the 1957-58 crop year.
The safeguards of the scheme are clear and definite. The chief one is the permit book in which will be recorded the cash advances that have been paid, and the elevator agent will be able to determine by an examination of the permit book whether or not an advance has been paid off. Responsibility for making the advance will rest with the elevator agent, and the agent must be reasonably sure that the farmer seeking the advance has on his farm the grain that must subsequently be delivered. In the third place, the farmer will be required to sign an affidavit in respect of the quantity of

grain available with respect to which he is seeking an advance, and I hope to deal with that question again when the opportunity presents itself. In the event I did not make it clear in my opening remarks I should reiterate that it is intended to have the cash advance system apply to wheat, oats and barley.
With regard to the financing of the scheme, that will be done in precisely the same way as at present when deliveries are made to an elevator, and shipments will be now entered with the wheat board and the offices of the elevator companies. With regard to the details of the financial aspect, we will be able to examine this in the committee stage.
The advance will be related to deliveries within a quota of 6 bushels per specified crop. The amount per bushel will be 50 cents for wheat, 20 cents for oats and 35 cents for barley. A ceiling of $3,000 will be set as the total that may be obtained by an applicant.
Now, to consider the size of the problem, the number of permit holders is approximately 231,000. Not every permit holder will require a cash advance, because conditions differ from area to area. I spoke about the unit quota. That is estimated to amount in total to 69 million bushels of wheat which will be complete in delivery very shortly, because the rate of marketing is approximately 30 million bushels per month.
With regard to the total amount of wheat that may be marketed in the course of the crop year, the estimate is based on the specified acreage and the returns from that acreage. It is expected that 372 million bushels would be the amount for which cash advances might be required. As each month proceeds deliveries are being made and the number of cash advances required will be correspondingly reduced. It is estimated, in so far as one can estimate in advance, that the total amount of money required for cash advances under the proposed plan may range from $100 million to $150 million. Repayment commences immediately as deliveries of grain are made, and in most instances will likely be completed within six or eight months. Interest charges as they accrue to the wheat board will be paid by the Minister of Finance out of the consolidated revenue fund, and administrative charges will be undertaken by the wheat board.
Those, Mr. Chairman, are the broad outlines of the plan for cash advances. I could have dealt at some considerable length with the wheat economy of western Canada and at this stage given the picture as I see it with regard to our wheat problem, but I thought at the resolution stage I would curtail my remarks. I know there are many hon. members in the house who are keenly interested 96698-23
Grain
in cash advances but who may prefer to discuss the subject on second reading or in the committee of the whole house after the printed bill is in their hands. If it is the wish of the house to complete the resolution stage today we could have the bill distributed this evening and proceed with second reading tomorrow, and on that occasion I would give a somewhat more complete account of our wheat problem. However, it is up to the good sense of the house as to what is required. We are prepared to discuss this at any stage and to any extent that hon. members may like.
In conclusion may I just say that the government is prepared to introduce this legislation at this time with confidence that its enactment will result in immediate benefit to agriculture. This measure is urgently required, and will be welcomed by thousands of farm families in western Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution which has just been moved by the Minister of Trade and Commerce is of course of necessity in very general terms. It provides:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the making of advances on account of initial payments for grain produced in the designated area-
-that area being, of course, the usual area covered by matters relating to the wheat board's operation, the three prairie provinces and including a part of British Columbia.
When we in the opposition formed the government party we dealt with this question over quite a considerable period of time, and we can fully understand why on this occasion the minister asked that the resolution be accepted now and that general discussion of the question take place at a later stage in the advancement of the measure through the house. I am not going to make any criticism of that, nor am I going to suggest it should be done otherwise, as has been the usual custom in connection with matters of this kind. There were, however, one or two remarks made in the short time the minister took to introduce the resolution upon which I think some comment should be made.
One of them was his statement to the effect that there are over 700 million bushels of carryover. It will be recalled by hon. members in general and by the minister in particular that when the announcement was made earlier in the season it was suggested that the figure for the carryover was something in excess of 600 million bushels. When a statement is made today that statistics indicate it is now over 700 million bushels, I would simply call attention to the fact that those who handle the grain-that is the three

Grain
pools in western Canada and the grain exchange in Winnipeg-were of the opinion that the figure of 700 million bushels was rather high. I believe they all issued statements to the effect that they did not think this figure was borne out by the facts. I believe it is important that attention should be called to that fact at this moment, although I am sure there will be other occasions during the session when we can be perhaps a little more critical of the figure which is said to be the carryover.
The criticism I made when I read that statement in the press for the first time was to the effect that the reason given for the necessity for the adjustment was that the bureau of statistics had made a mistake for each of the last five years, and I have just been wondering whether the calculations of those who have made a mistake for the last five years should be accepted without some examination into the facts to discover whether or not they are correct this time, particularly as all those who are handling the grain feel they are wrong. I think we should have it pretty well established at an early date just what the figure ought to be.
There is another point I wish to make at this time, and it is that there is nothing unexpected in the suggestions made in the resolution nor in the statement which has just been made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. As I have already pointed out, this is a subject which has been before the house on many previous occasions, and about which there has been considerable discussion.
But I am only going to refer to two of those occasions and only take a few words out of the statements which were made at the time to indicate the reason why there is no surprise when the statement is made at this time. When introducing amendments to the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act, a measure which had been on the statute books for some few years, the former minister of trade and commerce, the Right Hon. C. D. Howe, had this to say as found at page 2196 of Hansard of March 14, 1956:
We were asked to enact this legislation by every farm organization in western Canada. I had thought as a matter of fact that our grain legislation could very well be deferred until the autumn, when any steps we might take could be taken in the light of the coming season's crop results.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture, western section, met in Winnipeg about two months ago-
That would be in January.
-to discuss what it wanted the government to do and out of that meeting came just one request . . . There was a second meeting attended by representatives of every farm organization in Canada which was held in Saskatoon. The three wheat pools were represented, the federation of agriculture, the farmers' union and the United Grain Growers. From this meeting came just one request.

To pass on and leave out some of the details of the discussion, Mr. Howe went on to say:
Why did we not get other requests from these meetings? I am sure both meetings discussed cash advances. That is what both meetings were held for. We received no request for cash advances. Why? Because there was no agreement as to how such a plan could be administered. I am told there was the widest difference among various groups as to what they wanted by way of machinery for cash advances.
The proposed amendments were suggested to the house and following that an amendment was moved by the hon. member for Moose Mountain and these two matters were under consideration for some time. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Moose Mountain was in these words, as found at page 2699 of Hansard of March 26, 1957:
That Bill No. 263 he not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing legislation to provide a permanent system of cash advances on farm-stored grain.
I am not too sure as to how permanent the present proposal is but it might be taken to be a proposal to pay such advances on a somewhat permanent basis. But when the measure to amend the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act came up for discussion in the house, again the former minister of trade and commerce was quite clear in expressing his views with regard to the matter. The matter before the house on April 6, 1957 was the amendment of the hon. member for Moose Mountain together with the proposed amendments to the previous legislation brought in by the minister of trade and commerce. In discussing the matter in his final remarks to the house before the bill received final passage, Mr. Howe stated, as found at page 3210 of Hansard of April 6, 1957:
We have heard vague talk from the opposition about cash advances, free of interest, on farm-stored grain. Various people have suggested ways in which the cash could be put out but no one, as far as I have been able to follow the debate, has suggested any way in which such an advance could be recovered.
Mr. Chairman, I did have a meeting with representative farm organizations a month or so ago, and at that time those present urged that this legislation be passed.
That is the legislation providing for bank loans.
They said they were not ready to put forward any other plan at this time but that they might be in the autumn.
Of course, we have come to the autumn. Mr. Howe went on to point out that the proper time to give consideration to the matter would be in the autumn. He went on, as found at page 3210 of Hansard, to refer to the resolutions passed and wired him by the

Grain
farm organizations in that area of the country to the effect that the then government should again bring down the measure providing for loans from the banks, that they should double the amount and should change the date to the 1st of September. The measure brought down at that time took that action.
I only wish to emphasize at this time that the whole matter was to be reconsidered in the autumn. The only solution, the only plan I have ever heard of that was placed before the farm organizations of the west and the trade in general was a plan placed before them by the president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, Mr. John Wesson. Insofar as I can understand the legislation from the few remarks made today that proposal is identical to the one which is now being proposed by the government. Of course we will find out as we go along whether it is exactly identical. There may be some difference in the figures that it will be necessary to discuss but in principle I think it is the same thing.
From the remarks which I have read and which were placed on Hansard last spring it will be understood, of course, that no agreement was reached by those to whom Mr. Wesson made the proposal on the matter. I understand it was placed before the three western pools and the grain trade and there was some difference of opinion as to whether they were prepared to accept the procedure which I understand this legislation provides for and which has been outlined to us in those terms this afternoon. But apparently many of the same individuals representing the same organizations were in Ottawa at a meeting which was held about two weeks ago. I am inclined to think that the ideas that were presented to the government were ideas which would have been presented to any government that might have been here at this particular time.
I want to say to the members of the present government that if the measure turns out to be one of the nature I think it is, judging from what I know of the whole situation they are not likely to find very much opposition from this group in the house with regard to the bringing down of the legislation and it will be our intention to promote, as far as it is possible to do so, the early bringing down of the legislation in order that we may have an early look at it and be in a position to discuss it intelligently, having all the facts before us when we do. Therefore I am not going to attempt to go into the detail of it at present. I am only going to say that it is carrying out an intention which it was indicated to the house by the previous 96698-23i
minister of trade and commerce in March and April of this year would be carried out by the previous government.

My friend says we should have done that a year ago. We are hopeful when this legislation is brought down that it will provide for something along that line.
There is one thing I should like to say at this stage. There is no indication in the remarks of the minister, nor is there any indication in the resolution, as to the government's intention with regard to the legislation covered by Bill No. 263 of the last session or the legislation of the 1956 session entitled the Prairie Grain Producers' Interim Financing Act. I should like to suggest that as the government found that measure helpful in the early part of this marketing season, it could be helpful in the early part of any marketing season and, as a matter of fact, all through the marketing period. I am hopeful that legislation will not be repealed, and there is nothing to indicate that it is going to be repealed. I would suggest that there are obvious benefits which can come from that legislation which probably could not be taken advantage of by some farmers

Crain
under the legislation which is proposed. I would hope that we may have both measures on the statute books after this legislation is passed, and that from the two acts farmers may be able to get more cash than they have been able to get up to this time.
If the legislation is such as to provide that that will be the case, then I can assure the government the measure will be given most earnest consideration. We are hoping that it will do all that the government hopes to have it do. If it does, it can only be helpful to the farmers.
Having said that, I just want to conclude by saying we are hopeful, as the minister is. that the resolution will not be held up unreasonably long and that we may get along to the position where the bill can be distributed. After that is done I hope I will not find it necessary to say too much with regard to it in the remaining part of the session. But I can assure hon. members if I think there is any necessity for saying much about it, I will proceed to say it. At the moment, we will support the resolution.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as we in this
group understood the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, namely that the legislation would provide for cash advances through the elevator system and that the interest charges would be borne by the treasury, we naturally will support the bill if it includes those features. I was most interested as I am sure all members of the house were, in the statement made by the hon. member for Melville. He built up a case for himself, and he may not have convinced anyone else but apparently he convinced himself that if we had been so unfortunate in this country as to have as the minister of trade and commerce the former member for Port Arthur Rt. Hon. C. D. Howe there would have been placed before this house at this time legislation along the lines of the legislation now before us. This is a statement with which we cannot agree at all. It would seem to me that if the minister had converted himself to the idea that we should have a system of interest-free cash advances, I could only conclude that, on this subject at any rate, he has learned more since June 10 than in all the years before that. However, I am not too sure he has been converted, because after he made that statement he said that before he could assure the minister and the house they were going to vote for the bill they were going to have to take a careful look at it. We can say, on the basis of the statement made by the minister, that so long as the bill contains those provisions we are going to support it.

We are going to support this legislation because we have had a part, and I believe a very considerable part, along with farm organizations and members of parliament in other parties in this house, over the years in promoting the idea, in publicizing it and getting support for it. The idea was that when a farmer harvests his grain in the fall, when he can send it only to a government agency, which is his preference, and there is no opportunity because of congestion and the absence of markets to deliver his grain, then a responsibility falls upon the government which operates the marketing agency to provide a system for making payments to the producers.
We feel that because we have helped to pioneer this legislation-I remind the house that an amendement was moved by this group asking for cash advances as far back as 1951-we are to some extent responsible for this legislation now being placed before the House of Commons. I think we can take particular satisfaction from these two features because in the debate on this question in this house one year ago we were the first and only group for a matter of days to say that we were so much opposed to the idea of farmers being forced to pay interest on really what was their own money that we were prepared to oppose the bank loan legislation. Gradually, after some days of debate, other members from other parties came to that point of view. I believe that as a result of that work in this house we are now faced with the likelihood that farmers are going to have this advance in worth-while legislation.
We recognize, of course, that the legislation before us is not a solution to the agricultural problem that faces this country. While it is absolutely necessary, and must be a part of an orderly system of grain marketing to have in legislative form a system of interest-free cash advances, basically this is not much more than a measure to assist in times of very bad conditions. We are hopeful that the government will take the other basic and necessary steps that will result in an improvement to the whole of the agricultural economy.
The best interpretation I am able to place on the remarks of the hon. member for Melville is that he is waiting for the farm organizations. While he has assured nobody he will go as far as the farm organizations go, he will never go any farther than the farm organizations go. I am one who is prepared to do my own thinking. Although I am a member of, and a supporter of all the large farm organizations in western Canada, I believe that so far as the interest rate is concerned until recent days this

Grain
legislation has been in advance of the general conclusions of the farm organizations. I, for one, do not intend to be merely a spokesman in this house for a given farm organization. I am prepared to do my own thinking, and our group will advance legislation which we feel meets the situation.
So in this instance some leadership has been given. However, I thought the hon. member for Melville might have had some objections to this legislation because I can recall so vividly when he sat on the other side of the house with his colleagues that they rose time after time and said, "If you have any arrangement like this through the Canadian wheat board, it means the end of the Canadian wheat board; it cannot be done; it is a terrible thing." We even heard it said that if the government at the time had suggested this type of legislation all of the wheat board members would tender their resignations. It was just as much poppycock at that time as it would be to say it now. There is nothing to it.

speechtext: This is not what you are talking about today.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
We said that it should be
through the elevator system; the government said no. They wanted to do it through their friends, the chartered banks. There was no risk for the banks; there was a government guarantee. The farmers did not want it through the banks but that is the best the former administration could provide. There has been an almost complete collapse of many of the export markets that we formerly occupied. The former administration had no suggestions; they had no ideas.
It used to be that the Liberal party had some ideas. They used to be a party of promises and they went out in one election after another and made great promises. But in the past election they made no promises. They did not have an idea. They did not have a clue. When the Leader of the Opposition came to speak in the city of Regina in the recent election, what did he offer the farmers in what perhaps is considered to be the wheat capital of Canada in order to help them in this situation? He offered nothing. He did not have a single concrete offer.
However, he went over all of the moneys that the farmers had ever obtained through any legislation that the government had ever had anything to do with,-when it had given a guarantee to the banks and the farm loans,- he added it up and, if I remember correctly, came to the astronomic figure of $750 million that he said was the extent to which the government of the day was helping agriculture of this country. The farmers reached up and scratched their heads and said, "Well, we still
owe most of it. We are going to have to pay it." When he forces us to go to the banks now and to borrow the money and to pay interest on our credit, he comes out and tells us that it is part of the government's assistance program for farmers.
Hence the producers naturally took a great deal of objection to the attitude of that administration. That fact, of course, accounts in large measure for the fact that this once great, virile Liberal party is now the smallest of the parties in the four western provinces. With the record of the Liberal party in the past and the ineptitude of the members of the official opposition at this time it will not be at all surprising that, when the Manitoba election is over, the Liberal party, as far as western Canada is concerned, will be almost as extinct as the historic prairie buffalo. We do not expect much difficulty in doing what other members of this party have already said we shall do, namely being the real opposition and the effective alternative to the policies and the programs that may be advanced.
But after having said some complimentary things about this legislation, after having said that we are proud we have had a hand in bringing it forward, I want to impress upon the government that we are today in a period of great congestion as far as grain marketing is concerned. Right now we are probably in a period of lower quotas than we have seen for many years at this stage. In spite of the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, our markets for the current crop year do not compare favourably with our exports and markets in the previous year.
As far as the basic condition of agriculture today is concerned, the ability to get enough income to cover expenses and to provide the farmer with a living, there is no doubt about it that agriculture is worse off today than it was on that memorable occasion of June 10. The price-cost squeeze has continued. The basic conditions that over the last years have made it difficult for the farmers still exist, as far as I can see. We are seeing more and more inflation and a greater and greater rise in prices as the days go by, but we are not seeing any strengthening generally of agricultural prices. We are seeing instead a gradual but rather consistent deterioration of agricultural prices.
I know there are members in this house who think that the people from western Canada and from agricultural constituencies are just cry-babies and that we overestimate the difficulties which the agricultural industry faces. However, I want to remind hon. members of this fact. Since 1947 this industry

Crain
has experienced an increase in costs of 46 per cent, as far as western Canada is concerned, and a drop in agricultural prices of 8 per cent. What other industry in a 10-year period could survive an increase in costs of 46 per cent while they receive a reduction of 8 per cent in the price of products they had to sell? For the wheat producer the position is even worse because in the same period of time the price of wheat dropped even more. As far as the farmer is concerned, it dropped for average grade by 34 cents a oushel, from $1.63 to $1.29 per bushel.
What should be done to correct this difficulty that is facing agriculture? The present measure is welcome; it is necessary. But the thing which must be done now is to improve the prices of agricultural products. We are looking forward to the new legislation which we expect will be before the house before many days are past.
Let me suggest that the government at this time should consider establishing something for which the farm organizations have been campaigning for many years. I refer to the establishment of a domestic parity price for wheat. 1 suggest that the price should be not less than $2.25 a bushel. Lest people who are consumers of grain and consumers of bread and who are not in the production of grain think that such an increase would result in an astronomic rise in the price of bread, let me suggest that the increased cost would not amount to more than one cent per loaf. As I have read the resolutions of the Canadian Labour Congress; they have gone hand in hand with the farm organizations in this country in asking for a system of parity prices and a system of support prices that will give to the agricultural producer a reasonable standard of living.
I would suggest also that the government might consider the suggestion of farm organizations that a system of deficiency payments should be established. What the farm organizations mean by deficiency payments is a straight payment out of the national treasury to the people who produce these products. They say that if conditions are such that their prices are allowed to collapse until their industry is threatened, there should be a subsidy-call it deficiency payment or call it what you like-from the treasury to an extent necessary to keep this industry in existence. Of course, that is not a proposition that was put only to this government, it was put to the previous administration.
As to something that might be done immediately, I would suggest to the minister that he consider the immediate payment of

an interim sum of money. On the wheat market, on the 1956 to 1957 crops, farm organizations asked that this deficiency payment be amended to an interim payment of not less than 20 cents a bushel. Now the time for interim payments is getting late. We used to get the interim payments during the crop year through which we were passing and now the crop year has gone by. Year after year the interim and final payments are becoming later and later.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce may say to me that there really is not enough money in the fund, that the former administration juggled the accounts and did some slick bookkeeping in order to get a small final payment through just before the election came. Even if that is true, even if the former administration, in order to get the farmers' vote, did make a payment just before election, I suggest to the minister that nevertheless the request of the farm organizations for 20 cents per bushel, based on the present costs of production and on the present prices for agricultural products, is one that the government should consider.
I have mentioned the tremendous increase in the cost of production, and I have mentioned also the congestion in the country. I have here the latest figures from the Canadian wheat board statistical summary showing that in country elevators on October 9 there were some 37 million bushels more than in the previous year. Lakehead stocks were up, Pacific stocks- were up and there was general congestion. Now the general situation is just a little worse than it was a year ago.
I also have the figures of existing quotas in western Canada. The Minister of Trade and Commerce mentioned the unit quota which is in effect at the present time. The unit quota is a quota for only 300 bushels of wheat. Even if the wheat is of good grade it amounts to a sum of just $350. For the vast majority of wheat producers on the prairie and for the vast majority of the people who hold the
231.000	permit books of which the minister spoke, that is the sum of money they have received since August 1. Three hundred and fifty dollars to pay their taxes, to pay their fuel bill, to pay their repair accounts, to pay their store accounts. That situation is demonstrated by the fact that out of just over
2.000	delivery points on October 17 there were 1,547 still on the unit quota and just 497 had advanced to the one bushel quota first specified; a very serious and a very difficult situation. Their income in the past has not been great because our exports last year were at a low point. The minister said that in August we were just a little above the American exports. Let us hope that our

Grain
relative position will improve because last year, while we exported 262.8 million bushels of wheat the United States in the same period exported 541.6 million bushels of wheat, more than twice as much as we exported from this country.
That is the general situation-a price-cost squeeze, tremendous congestion and a substantial falling off in markets. This government has suggested two positive things; one is this legislation and the other is a resolution which foreshadows legislation to support it. However, this government has made other statements and has informed us of other attitudes in the last few weeks which I suggest are rather disturbing and which paint the picture of the real situation and the basic attitude of the government.
One of the clauses and one of the provisions in this legislation is that the advance will be made on a six bushel quota. A six bushel quota is a small quota; a six bushel quota is very little more than the farmers marketed last year, so what the minister is saying in this legislation is that this government, with its visits to Washington and with every other thing it might be trying to do to improve our exports, so far as making a cash advance is concerned and as far as this legislation is concerned-and that is the proof of their thinking-are not certain that they are going to be able to export any more than in previous years. Well that is very disturbing. The farm organizations have asked for an advance on at least an eight bushel quota. That has been their general attitude in years gone by. We in this group would like to see an advance made on all of the grain held by these family farms but that is the best the government is doing in this legislation.
We had an intimation yesterday from the Minister of Finance that the government has done no new thinking as to how it might increase exports. When somebody asked the minister whether the government had considered taking sterling he said "nobody has asked us and therefore we have not made any such suggestion." Well that is one of the suggested new policies which have been advanced from time to time and one of the things that I believe could be of real benefit to this country.
Many ministers in this government in the last few weeks have made statements which led a lot of us to hope there would be a great expansion in the Colombo plan, there would be much more money placed at the disposal of the plan and that a great part of this large increase would be used for the purchase of food. We had an announcement the other day that there was going to be an
increase and it would be from $34,400,000 to $35 million, scarcely an increase at all. I wondered if the government had not learned anything from the increase given by the former administration to the old age pensioners, that a small and inadequate increase does not gain either sympathy or support for the administration. That is another opportunity this government has lost.
I believe it was yesterday that I asked the Minister of Agriculture whether or not his government was prepared to reverse the attitude of the former administration towards an international food bank with the idea of an international commodity clearing house. He said the government has no different policy or has not made up its mind in that regard-

Mr. Chairman, there has been large scale dissatisfaction in western Canada over the guaranteed loans to farmers by the chartered banks, provided for by legislation. The farmers did not want an opportunity to plunge further into debt. They did not want to have to borrow; they wanted to be able to sell, and in the fall of 1955 there were large protest meetings at which farmers asked the government to pass legislation to make advances against grain held on the farms.
1 cannot help being somewhat amused by the sidestepping of the former minister of agriculture when he told us that the farm organizations had met and had only passed one resolution-apparently they did not pass one regarding cash advances. But, of course, he just picked out the particular farm organization he wanted to pick out. Let me remind him that the interprovincial farm union council asked about cash advances some two years ago. They presented a brief in this house on February 16, 1956, and I will read the resolution.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member is putting words into my mouth. I read out of Hansard what he is going to answer, and the record is there, and I referred to the page for any one to read it.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
Yes. The hon. member kept referring to the fact that certain farm organizations had met and had not asked for advances. But on February 16 the interprovincial farm union council brief contained this passage:
The interprovincial farm union council is continuing to press for adoption of its original proposal, which has been endorsed at the three wheat pool delegate meetings, that the government arrange for interest-free cash advances by the Canadian wheat board on farm-stored grain to the value of 50 per cent of the initial payment on an estimated delivery of eight bushels per cultivated acre.
I want to congratulate the present government for having introduced the present resolution. Apparently it only provides for advances on a quota of 6 bushels to the acre. I am sure the minister will agree that it is going to be very hard for farmers to finance on the basis of even an 8-bushel quota to the acre, and if he cuts the advance

down to an amount on 6 bushels to the acre it is going to make it that much harder. I hope therefore he will give consideration to raising it from six to eight. I am not suggesting we should go as far as the hon. member for Assiniboia has suggested when he said advances should be made against all the grain on the farm. I have not heard any farm organization meetings-and I have attended a very large number of meetings in the constituencies-which have once suggested that.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: May I remind the hon. member, for whom we all have great respect, that I was speaking of a family farm. I was not suggesting that it should apply in the case of huge farms; there should be some acreage limitation.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
Even so, there is a good reason, I think, why that suggestion would not be sound, and this is the reason; it is one that was brought to my attention by farmers at meeting after meeting. They said: we should like an advance on all the grain on our farms but we realize that if the government were to make advances against all the grain there would have to be very close inspection, and the cost would be prohibitive, so it would be better to leave a wide margin so that advances can be made without inspection at very little cost. To try to make the advance against the total amount of grain held on the farm would, I think, wreck the whole proposal.
Mr. Chairman, some people ask why should we make advances against grain and not against other farm commodities? Of course, the reason is obvious. Grain and wheat are in a congested state; farmers cannot sell their crops and, therefore, they need advances. In addition to that, the price of wheat is lower than the price of practically any other farm commodity. The price today is less than 70 per cent of parity on the basis used by the Agricultural Prices Support Act, 1943-45. On the basis of that, the parity price would be around $2.37 a bushel.
I want to make it absolutely clear that I am not in any way criticizing the Canadian wheat board for their handling of wheat. I think they have done an exceptionally good job, and they have done it under very severe handicaps.
I say they have operated under extremely severe handicaps because they have had to face unfair competition in the world markets. They have had to pay the farmers on the basis of world prices while practically every other country has subsidized the price of wheat. For that reason I think the request of 96698-24
Grain	*
the interprovincial farm union for a deficiency payment of 20 cents a bushel on the 1956-57 crop is a fair one. Even then it would leave the price of wheat considerably below that of the parity price. But even worse than that situation is the fact that the wheat board has been forced to sell through the normal channels of trade whilst their main competitor, the United States, has been selling wheat and accepting payment in foreign currencies and by barter. As a consequence of that we have lost a number of our markets.
Not satisfied with placing the wheat board under the two handicaps I have mentioned the government in the past added another handicap by making the wheat board demand payment in an appreciated currency, a currency at a premium of four cents which meant that the farmers lost approximately seven cents a bushel as a result of that appreciated currency on the basis of par. Let us compare that with what happened in 1950 when the Canadian dollar was held at a value of 90 cents as compared with the United States dollar. Compared with that situation the farmers today are losing 27 cents a bushel as a result of the appreciated value of the dollar.
I am suggesting that if the government considers it sound from a national point of view to maintain the dollar at an appreciated level, if the general economy as a whole benefits by so doing, then the farmers would be absolutely justified in asking that they be compensated to the amount of seven cents a bushel to make up their loss as a result of the government's financial policy.
The former minister of trade and commerce blamed the unsatisfactory condition of agriculture upon a succession of good crops which of course created surpluses and forced the price of wheat down. We insist that the former government must accept the full responsibility for that bad situation as it depended upon orthodox channels of trade to sell its commodities and as a consequence we lost markets.
Whilst the former government followed this policy of laissez faire our main competitors opened up new channels of trade and step by step succeeded in diverting sales of wheat from Canada to the United States, and as a consequence our sales have fallen off and our surpluses have accumulated. The former minister of trade and commerce was asked on a number of occasions whether he thought the farmers should reduce their production of grain. It was suggested to the government that the success of its policy depended largely upon crop failures. I recall

Grain
that the former minister of trade and commerce said in this house he hoped that in western Canada we would harvest a bumper crop which would have further added to the government's difficulties in disposing of our wheat.
Then he said the government considered it wise to maintain a substantial reserve of wheat on hand so that in the event of a succession of crop failures it would have a reserve of wheat to meet our domestic needs and the needs of other nations. I think the minister was justified in that attitude at that time because it had been pointed out to us time and time again by the Food and Agriculture Organization that 50 per cent of the population of the world was still unfed and hungry and therefore if there had been a succession of crop failures we might very well have had world wide famine.
If the government considers it to be in the national interest to maintain a substantial reserve of wheat on hand then undoubtedly it should be a national responsibility to provide storage to handle that reserve so that it may be held without its interfering with the normal handling of the current crop, it should be a national responsibility to pay the carrying charges on that reserve and it should also be a national responsibility to make advances against grain held on a farm when due to the fact that the reserve is plugging the channels through which the grain moves the farmers are unable to deliver their grain.
I believe that the situation could have been eased last year and could be eased even now to some extent by the government reconsidering what is apparently its decision not to license off-site storage. I was not satisfied with the reply given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce yesterday and I am not blaming him because after all the government has been in office only a short time and has inherited a lot of policies of the former government which up to the present time they have not had a chance to modify.
Let us examine the reasons given for refusing to license off-site storage. It was argued that the grain in off-site storage might deteriorate. I read a report issued by the Alberta wheat pool last year which said that the amount of deterioration in off-site storage was infinitesimal, that the grain in off-site storage was being carried just as efficiently and well as grain in the elevators.
It was also argued by the government that grain in off-site storage would not be as accessible as grain in elevators. I would say that grain in off-site storage would be just about as accessible as grain held in annexes

that have no auger because grain held in annexes of this kind has to be loaded up into a truck and moved into the elevator. When you consider that as a rule off-site storage is only a few yards from the elevator it cannot seriously be argued that grain held in off-site storage is not accessible.
I am sorry the government has decided not to license off-site storage because by such an action it is destroying the initiative of the farmers and local business people. I think there is a great deal of credit due the farmers and local businessmen when they have provided buildings in which grain can be stored. The building is then leased to an elevator company and more grain can be delivered.
There is no reason why the wheat board should be too concerned about whether or not grain held in off-site storage will deteriorate because if there is any loss involved it is the local elevator company rather than the wheat board which must sustain the loss because it has to deliver the same type of wheat as that which it accepts into storage. I am sure no local elevator company is going to agree to rent a building which it does not consider satisfactory for the storage of grain.
I am afraid there is another reason why the government refuses to license off-site storage. I think the obvious reason is because it has agreed to paying the carrying charges on the wheat and just the minute it accepts grain into off-site storage it has to pay the storage charges on it to the extent that the total storage is in excess of 187 million bushels. I believe that is the real reason the government refuses to license off-site storage because it does not want to increase its payments for storage.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has suggested that perhaps there should be a reduction in wheat acreage. I listened very carefully to what he said just now. I am of the impression that the Minister of Agriculture has also made a somewhat similar statement to the effect that it might be wise to divert certain acreage from the producion of wheat to the production of livestock.
But I think one has got to be extremely careful how one attempts to do that because the result could very easily be a surplus of livestock and a surplus of livestock will be far more difficult to handle than a surplus of grain. We have had that experience in the past with hogs. We know what happens when we have a surplus of hogs. You cannot hold them. They have got to move when they are at a certain weight and the result

Grain
is that you completely wreck the market. Therefore we have got to be very careful in that regard unless we are prepared to adopt some such proposal as the soil bank in the United States. Personally I am not advocating that because I do not believe there is any necessity of reducing acreage. In the light of the world situation today, with 50 per cent of the population of the world undernourished, our problem is to find ways and means of getting the wheat to the people who are hungry.
I think the United States today is giving a wonderful example of how surplus food can be got to hungry people. Instead of worrying about reducing acreage, let the government explore every means of getting our surplus wheat to nations who are unable to obtain it through the normal channels of trade. Let the government make that wheat available to them for their own currency or by barter or, in the case of absolute distress, by gift. It would be far better to make that wheat available by gift than to reduce the acreage. If letting these people have our wheat meant that somebody in this country had to go without I would not make the suggestion, but there is no suggestion that anyone would be penalized as the result of making such gifts.
The first thing is to accept foreign currency, especially sterling, and use that sterling for the purchase of commodities in the sterling area which we are purchasing at the present time from the United States. I am encouraged to hope that the government may give consideration to that proposal because I recall that on December 3, 1953, the present Prime Minister voted in support of the acceptance of sterling. Therefore I am hoping that the Conservative government may even yet consider the desirability of such action.
We in this group have argued ever since 1952 that farm produce should be sold in this country under a two-price system, that is that farm commodities sold in the domestic market should be sold at a parity price and our exports at the best price obtainable. By "parity price" we merely mean a price that bears a fair relationship to the price of other commodities. We believe that should be the policy in regard to wheat and wheat that is to be exported should be sold preferably through the international wheat agreement or at least supported at a price that bears a fair relationship to cost. Then to the extent that the total price received by the farmers for agricultural produce gives them an income less than their fair share, deficiency payments might very well be made.
There is a good reason why grain growers have the right to expect better consideration
96698-24i
than they have received in the past. Let us not forget that shortly after the war the government of that day signed the British wheat agreement and they said that was to be regarded as a form of stabilization. Let us not forget that as the result of the British wheat agreement the farmers of this country lost $431 million representing the difference between what they would have received on the world market and the price they received under the British wheat agreement. But not only that, they sold wheat in the domestic market for the same price which meant a loss to the farmers of another $136.9 million. All in all, as the result of the government wheat policy in those days, the farmers during that period lost a total of $568 million.
I know that many people are under the delusion that the grain producers of this country have been subsidized. The grain producers have never been subsidized. They sold at world market prices. The only government in the world that forced farmers to accept less than the world market price was the Liberal government of the past. In view of the fact that the farmers of this country subsidized Canadian consumers for a number of years to the extent of $136 million they have a right to look upon that $136 million as a premium that they paid on a form of insurance that guaranteed that they would get fair prices in the future. Therefore the farmers have every right today to expect the government to stabilize the price of grain at a fair level along with other farm commodities.
I am glad to see the government bringing down this legislation. I am glad to hear that the government is going to bring down additional legislation regarding support prices. I do not expect the government to redress all the evils of the former government. The former government showed a total lack of appreciation of the welfare of the farmers and I am hoping that in the next few months this government will be able to undo a lot of the evil that the former government did.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think that at the present time the people of Canada are more concerned about what they are going to get in the way of legislation from the present government than they are about trying to find fault with what has happened during the last several years. The people of Canada were asked to pass a verdict on June 10 and they voted for more members representing the party of the then opposition than they did for those representing the former government, indicating that they believed the promises made by the present Prime Minister and thought they were worthy of support. Therefore I suggest that what the people of Canada

Grain
are interested in now is to what extent the Prime Minister and the government are prepared to go to carry out the promises held out to the people by the Prime Minister and on the basis of which he holds his present office. In my opinion the government will be judged by the extent to which they justify the hopes that they raised when they were asking for support at that time.
My purpose this afternoon is to indicate what I think the people of western Canada were led to expect from the statements of the present Prime Minister in regard to this very matter and to indicate that I hope the bill goes some substantial way toward meeting those hopes and promises. I think that is what we have a right to expect when the government acts in a matter about which it has taken a very definite stand in the past. In that regard I wish to refer to what the present Prime Minister said on March 14, 1957 as recorded on page 2188 of Hansard. There the present Prime Minister spoke in these words:
Mr. Chairman, the amendments that are provided for in the resolution now before this committee were set forth yesterday by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in these words as reported at page 2161 of Hansard:
"... that the maximum amount of loan to an Individual producer be raised from $1,500 to $3,000; second, that the rate of interest, which is 5 per cent at present, be left to the determination of the governor in council; and loans be extended by one month by moving the opening date forward from October 1 to September 1."
The Prime Minister went on to say:
That in general represents the changes that are to be made when the bill is brought before the house. I believe that what is being done here represents a complete disregard of the wishes and requirements of all western farm organizations and of farmers throughout westen Canada.
As found at page 2189 of Hansard the present Prime Minister went on to say:
Those in general summarize the arguments that we in this party have advanced through the hon. member for Calgary North and the hon. member for Brandon-Souris. They represent the stand we have taken since 1952. We believe that the only salvation for the western farmer, with his markets lost and his wheat therefore unmarketable, is that there should be cash advances. Second, we believe that every encouragement should be given to the farmer to provide his own storage, and that in the provision of such storage additional write-offs should be permitted when determining the amount of his income tax.
We believe that under proper circumstances there should be provision for cash advances on farm-stored grain similar to the system in effect in the United States.
There was a definite pronouncement in the house by the present Prime Minister on behalf of his party. I am waiting with great anticipation to see if this bill puts in force any system of cash advances on farm-stored grain similar to the system in effect in the United States. It seems to me that the suggestion

of the Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon of permitting a maximum advance up to $3,000 is not in accordance with the hopes held out to the farmers at the time the present government was appealing for support.
Just look at what it amounts to, Mr. Chairman. Certainly, the average farm would not be bigger than three quarter sections. Supposing the specified acreage on such a farm were 400 acres. The amount of help which a farmer could get under this proposal would be $1,200. He then has to repay half of the amount he gets from any grain subsequently delivered. He would only be able to deliver these six bushels per specified acre over a period of a year, and assuming he takes a full year to deliver it he probably has, on an average, $600 for perhaps nine months. But, supposing one figures he has $900 for the whole year? What does this proposal mean? The only thing he gets out of it is firstly that it will be easier to get the money from the elevators than from the banks. And, as I understand the proposal, secondly to cancel the interest on that small amount. Today the farmer is in a much worse position than he was on June 10, and certainly far worse than he was a year ago, yet the measure of relief held out by the present government is the cancellation of interest which will not amount to more than $40 or $45, on an average.
So there may be no mistake as to what the people of western Canada really expected of the present government, let me read some more of what the present Prime Minister said, as reported at page 2188 of Hansard for March 14, 1957:
For several years we in this party have been supporting the need for cash advances. In 1952, as reported in Hansard for December 17 of that year, Hon. George Drew, then leader of the opposition, supported an amendment which had been moved recommending legislation providing for the payment to producers in respect of farm-stored grain of an advance equal to 75 per cent of the initial price established August 1 in each crop year.
I believe the initial price then was $1.20, it might have been $1.40, and this proposal would result in the payment of around 90 cents a bushel. I continue quoting:
Our only change over the passing years has been that while 75 per cent was the amount asked for at that time, the demand since has been generally that 50 per cent should be advanced. That demand has been universal, and in the face of that demand the bringing in of a loan system again is a denial of the wishes of farmers everywhere.
Now, what do we have proposed today? The proposal was scaled down to 50 per cent of the initial advance. Supposing you take the initial advance at $1.40, less the charges to Fort William which would get it down to

Grain
$1.20; 50 per cent of that is 60 cents a bushel, not 50 cents as proposed. But it goes farther than that. There was no idea, as I understand it, of restricting the basis of advance to six bushels per specified acre. What I think many people in western Canada had in mind as proposed was what the present Prime Minister had said himself, a system of cash advances like that in force in the United States. There was no rigid low limit there such as the limit of $3,000 proposed here. Under the proposed set-up the farmer is to get no more than $3,000 and that is to be repaid out of his deliveries so that at the end of the year actually he will be no better off than under the present system by means of which he could also get $3,000. It was to be repaid in the same way from deliveries of grain.
The Prime Minister referred to what Mr. Drew had said on the matter, and said the only change was a reduction from 75 per cent to 50 per cent. Here is what Mr. Drew said, as referred to by the Prime Minister, and as found at page 858 of Hansard for December 17, 1952. The amendment to the amendment to which Mr. Drew was speaking was:
To recommend legislation providing for the payment to producers, in respect to farm-stored grain, of an advance equal to 75 per cent of the initial price as established at August 1 in each crop year.
In dealing with this subamendment the former leader of the opposition, Mr. Drew, said:
In eifect this subamendment does two things. It is a proposal that legislation be introduced to provide for a cash advance to producers in respect of their farm-stored grain equal to 75 per cent of the initial payment the producer would have received if he had been able to deliver that grain to an agency of the wheat board.
There is no suggestion there that it should be only on six bushels per specified acre. It speaks about "that grain" and "the grain on hand". Then, Mr. Drew referred to his own remarks in the early stages of the same debate, and he quotes his own remarks. I again call your attention to the fact, Mr. Chairman, that the present Prime Minister referred to this statement and said that the only change that would be made by them was to reduce the payment from 75 per cent to 50 per cent. Here is what Mr. Drew said:
The whole system of handling and distribution has broken down. The government, no matter what its explanation may be, has failed to take effective steps to provide for the handling of grain, in spite of the knowledge many months ago, and the warnings many months ago, that this situation was going to arise. In western Canada today there are many farmers, with huge quantities of wheat and other grains worth considerable sums of money, who are unable to get money at this time to cover their harvesting and living expenses because of their inability to deliver that grain to market.
This is a situation with which the government should deal immediately. It is urgent and calls for attention without delay.
I call your attention, Mr. Chairman, to the idea held out to the farmers at that time. It was that many farmers who had huge quantities of wheat on hand should be able to turn that wheat into cash, and this was something that should be dealt with without delay. There appeared to be no idea of restricting it to six bushels, no idea of restricting it to $3,000. When the suggestion was made by the former administration to help the individual farmer to the extent of a loan of $3,000, the present Prime Minister felt very dissatisfied. He said this at page 2188 of Hansard for March 14, 1957:
I summarize our attitude towards this resolution and the bill to be founded thereon-
The bill being referred to was to give help up to $3,000. I admit the help was to be given through the banks and the farmers preferred to deal through the elevator companies, but what does this present proposal do? Does it give more than $3,000? Does it provide that they can have money until they deliver their wheat? They have to pay the debt off within a year if they can deliver up to six bushels an acre. The only thing accomplished by this proposal is merely a rebate of interest. Here is what the present Prime Minister had to say about the earlier proposal:
I summarize our attitude toward this resolution and the bill to be founded thereon as follows. What is being given to the farmer is a stone when he is asking for bread, and what is being provided under this resolution is something unwanted by the farmer, something totally ineffective to meet his needs, and something which in effect will be inoperative, as was the legislation to a large extent during the past year.
I cite that passage to the present Prime Minister-they are his own	words-in
regard to this former bill. He said, "It is totally inadequate". Is $3,000 today more adequate than it was a year ago? I wonder. This was said to be a stone a year ago or less. It was said to be a stone on March 14. According to the words of the present leader of the government, "What is being provided is something unwanted by the farmer". I submit that the farmer wanted help then; he wants help now. But after all the speeches that were made to him on the floor of this house by the former leader of the Progressive Conservative party, endorsed by the present Prime Minister, he expected more help than this proposal of an advance which he must pay back within a year, limited to $3,000 and also limited to the extent of 50 cents a bushel on wheat and to the extent of 6 bushels an acre on his specified acreage.

I am discussing the principle of the bill. It goes such a short distance that I am just pointing it out for the edification of my hon. friends. Let me read again what the Prime Minister held out and express the hope that he will yet reconsider and make this bill into something more in line with the needs of western Canada and more in line with the hopes he held out when those neighbours of both his and mine voted for him. Here is what he said, as reported at page 2189 of Hansard of March 14, 1957:
. . . the only salvation for the western farmer, with his markets lost and his wheat therefore unmarketable, is that there should be cash advances.
Is this such a cash advance measure when you can get up to $3,000 which is taken back from you within a year and can market only up to six bushels per specified acre? Is this the solution which the Prime Minister had in mind?
Is it to be said that after what happened to them in their attempt at Washington to
get some reconsideration of the surplus disposal policy of the United States that they the government really expect any great amelioration of the marketing problem? The situation is still there, just the same and worse.
Then the Prime Minister has said there should be cash advances; now this is really a temporary advance, repayable within a year. Is this going to really help our farmers in the way in which they were led to believe they would be helped? The Prime Minister said:
We believe that every encouragement should be given to the farmer to provide their own storage and that with the provision of such storage, additional writeoffs should be permitted when determining the amount of his income tax.
I hope that the government will carry out that promise.
It was suggested from time to time that that should be done right in the Wheat Board Act so there would be no doubt about it but, in any event, this is something which should be done at this session of parliament and without delay, because the situation in western Canada is very difficult as the Prime Minister very well knows. I would like the government to give consideration to this question and the Minister of Trade and Commerce can answer it if he wishes to do so: does he seriously suggest that this proposal he has just made carries out the promises of the Prime Minister who said: "We believe that under proper circumstances there should be provision for cash advances on farm-stored grain similar to the system in effect in the United States."
